name: Erik Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Brook Farm, the Hendersons' place, about two hundred acres of grass and barley with sixty beef cattle and a flock of ewes. Mornings I check the stock and feed round, then from ten I'm usually in the farm shop out by the road, cutting meat and serving. Afternoons it's back on the old Massey, fencing, hauling bales, whatever's broken that day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the shop more than I thought I would. Mrs Pike comes in every Thursday for two lamb chops and tells me which of our fields she walked her dog past, and she knows the animals by sight. What wears me out is the pay. I'm on a bit over minimum, and every winter the Hendersons say they'll look at it in spring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are you doing for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Me and my girlfriend Lena rent a flat above the hardware shop in the village. She's a teaching assistant at the primary school. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any time, and the car is fifteen years old, so every noise it makes is a small heart attack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, keep it as a search engine. I don't use any of it and I don't plan to. Lena uses one to make worksheets for the kids, and that's her business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing for me, and that's what I want. The farm runs on what it ran on twenty years ago, mostly. My worry in this picture is the same old one, which is that farm work is paid badly and nobody seems to care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. Ask for the raise again in March, try to get Mr Henderson to put the shop hours on a proper contract, and keep the car alive. Maybe do the chainsaw ticket, the safety certificate, because the council pays you extra for hedge work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, because calm here means still being skint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody seems to care about farm pay. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets, mostly, and the government that lets them squeeze. Our shop sells a pack of mince for what it costs to make, and the big store in town sells it for less because they buy from a place with ten thousand cattle. There should be a floor on what farmers get paid, same as there's a floor on wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you got that raise in March, what's the first thing it would go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tyres. All four of them are bald and I know it. Then I'd like to put a hundred a month by, so I stop checking my bank app at the till in the shop next door.

S0.say: I'd tell people to keep AI as a search engine, because I don't use it and don't plan to. Lena uses it for school worksheets and that's up to her.
S0.think: Privately I think this picture changes nothing for me, which is what I want. The real problem stays the same: farm work is paid badly and the supermarkets squeeze prices down.
S0.do: Asks again for a raise in March and pushes for the shop hours to go on a proper contract. Considers doing the chainsaw safety certificate for paid council hedge work, and plans to put a hundred a month aside if pay goes up.
S0.feel: Calm but flat. Nothing changes, which also means he stays short of money.
S0.quote: All four of them are bald and I know it.
S0.fieldNote: He was happiest talking about Mrs Pike and the shop, which tells me the customer side matters to him more than the machinery. The anger is aimed at supermarkets and weak rules, not at technology. He wants nothing new; he wants the old work paid properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like what happens anyway, just slower. People would nod at the pub. I'd probably say something like at least they're giving us time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer beginners is the bit that gets me. I only got this job because Mr Henderson took a chance on a lad from the college with a certificate and no experience. If farms stop doing that, the young ones end up in the warehouse on the ring road instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much different from now. I'd keep my head down and do my job well. If the Hendersons bought some new gadget for the shop, like a till that does the stock count for you, I'd let someone else learn it first and pick it up off them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Not for me so much, for the kid I was at nineteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a young person you'd be thinking about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Jonas. He's seventeen and wants to farm, and he's good with sheep, better than me at lambing already. If nobody hires beginners, he's stuck. I'd ask the Hendersons to take him on for summers at least, even if they paid him in meat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let someone else learn the new gadget first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what happens when you rush. The Hendersons bought a card machine that kept losing signal, and for a month I was writing card numbers on a pad. I'll learn it when it works. I'm not against new things, I just don't trust them on day one.

S1.say: I'd say it sounds like what happens anyway, only slower. At least we'd have time to see it coming.
S1.think: What worries me is farms hiring fewer beginners, because a farmer took a chance on me when I had nothing but a certificate. If that stops, young people end up in warehouses instead.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and lets others learn any new shop technology before him. Asks the Hendersons to give his seventeen-year-old cousin Jonas summer work.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, more for young people starting out than for himself.
S1.quote: He's seventeen and wants to farm, and he's good with sheep, better than me at lambing already.
S1.fieldNote: The worry turned outward to his cousin straight away, which fits his progressive leanings. He was clear that waiting before trying new tools isn't hostility but caution from a bad experience with a card machine. Slow, careful, protective of the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it serves the office lot right for telling us for years to get a proper job. No, I wouldn't say that, that's mean. I'd say they need a union, same as we do, and the government should make the companies pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deep down I think it's not my fight, at first. Nobody's going to put an assistant on my fencing. But Lena's sister works at the bank in town, and if she gets laid off she'll be on our sofa within a month. That's where it reaches us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena we need to start a proper savings pot, even fifty a month. I'd sign the union petitions and maybe go to the meeting in the town hall if there's one. I'd also put the Thursday meat boxes on a list on paper, so if office people start watching every penny I know who's dropping off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see it coming down the road even though it's not at my gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said office people might watch every penny. What would that do to the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop runs on people who can afford to pay a bit more for local meat. Half our Saturday customers are commuters who stop on the way home. If they lose their jobs, they go back to the supermarket mince, and I'm cutting meat nobody buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use one of these assistants yourself, say for the shop orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know Lena would say it's quicker, and maybe it is. But the orders are in my head and in my notebook, and I don't want a machine knowing what Mrs Pike buys every week. Call me old-fashioned at twenty-seven.

S2.say: I'd say office workers need a union just like farm workers do. The government should make companies pay for retraining the people they let go.
S2.think: At first I think it's not my fight, because no assistant is going to do my fencing. But if Lena's sister loses her bank job she'll be living with us, and if commuters lose their jobs the shop loses its best customers.
S2.do: Starts a savings pot of about fifty a month with Lena. Signs union petitions, goes to a town hall meeting if there is one, and keeps a paper list of the regular meat box customers to spot who drops off.
S2.feel: Uneasy, watching a problem come closer without it reaching him yet.
S2.fieldNote: He took back his first, sharper remark himself, which I read as honest rather than staged. The link he drew between office jobs and the shop's Saturday trade was the most concrete moment. Refuses the tools on privacy grounds as much as habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, plain and simple. If share prices boom while people lose their jobs, then tax the shares and pay for the people. I'd say that at the pub and I'd say it online, and I'd get shouted at for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, house prices booming scares me more than the AI. We've been saving for a deposit in theory for three years, and in this picture that dream just ends. We'd rent above the hardware shop until we're fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join a party for the first time, probably, and go to meetings. I'd ask the Hendersons straight out whether they'd ever rent me one of the farm cottages, because the old one by the barn is empty. And I'd keep going to work, because in this picture my hands are the safe bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and angry in a way I don't like. My work's safe but my life gets smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you said that about taxing shares at the pub, who'd shout at you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave from the feed merchants, for a start. He'd say I want to punish people for doing well. I'd tell him I just want the person who lost their job in the bank to still afford a pack of our sausages. We've had that argument before about other things and we still drink together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your hands are the safe bit here. Does that feel like good news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, but no. It feels like being told you're safe because nobody wants what you've got. The money's going to the people with shares and houses, and I've got a pair of boots and a girlfriend I can't buy a house with.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be shared and that big share profits should be taxed to support the people losing work. I'd say it in the pub and online, knowing people would shout back.
S3.think: Privately the house price boom scares me more than the AI, because it would end any hope of a deposit. My work is safe, but my life gets smaller.
S3.do: Joins a political party for the first time and goes to meetings. Asks the Hendersons whether he could rent the empty farm cottage by the barn, and keeps working as normal.
S3.feel: Anxious and angry, safe at work but shut out of owning a home.
S3.quote: It feels like being told you're safe because nobody wants what you've got.
S3.fieldNote: His fear moved from jobs to housing in this one, and he saw clearly that being 'untouched' isn't the same as gaining. The argument with Dave was told with affection, not bitterness. Joining a party would be a big step for someone this cautious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ban them from farms unless a person's in charge, and tax every robot like it's a worker. That's what I'd say, loudly. I'd be at the protest with a sign Lena made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done in this one. The Hendersons aren't rich, and if a robot can feed round and do fencing for less than me, they'll do the sums. Mr Henderson would hate it, he'd apologise, and he'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fight to keep the shop job, because I think people still want a person behind the meat counter. I'd ask to go full-time in the shop and drop the field work before they drop me. And I'd start looking at the abattoir in the next town, because a robot can't do that one gently yet, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. It's the first one where I can picture the day I'm told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you picture that day? Where would you be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the yard by the shop, probably on a Monday, because that's when Mr Henderson does the books. He'd say something like we need to talk, lad, and he'd look at his boots. Then I'd drive home and sit in the car outside the hardware shop for a while before going up to tell Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people still want a person at the meat counter. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, honestly. Mrs Pike would want me. The commuters on Saturday might not care, if a machine was cheaper and quicker. But I've got to believe in something, and that counter's the thing I've got.

S4.say: I'd say robots should be banned from farms unless a person is in charge, and taxed as if they were workers. I'd be at the protest with a sign.
S4.think: Privately I think I'm finished in this one, because the Hendersons aren't rich and would do the sums. Mr Henderson would hate it and apologise, but he'd still do it.
S4.do: Asks to move full-time into the farm shop before the field work goes. Starts looking at the abattoir in the next town as a backup, and joins protests calling for a robot tax.
S4.feel: Properly scared. For the first time he can picture the day he's told.
S4.quote: Then I'd drive home and sit in the car outside the hardware shop for a while before going up to tell Lena.
S4.fieldNote: This was the turn where the calm went. The picture of Monday book-keeping and Mr Henderson looking at his boots came fast, as if he'd imagined it before. His plan rests on the shop counter, and he admitted he isn't sure it holds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, no contest. The others hurt other people first and reach me second. What would help is a robot tax that pays farm workers to retrain, and a rule that small farms get help to keep people on, not just grants to buy machines. Grants always go to the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals, or the customers. Mrs Pike doesn't buy lamb chops from us because they're cheap. She buys them because she knows me and she knows the field. If that stops mattering to people, then I don't know what we've been doing all this time.

headlineQuote: It feels like being told you're safe because nobody wants what you've got.
portrait: Erik Bauer is a 27-year-old farm worker on Brook Farm, a mixed beef, sheep and barley farm with a roadside shop where he cuts meat and serves. He rents a flat in the village with his girlfriend Lena, a teaching assistant, and they usually have about two weeks of money saved. He never uses AI tools and prefers to let others learn new technology first. Through the early pictures he stays calm and blames supermarkets and weak rules for low farm pay; in the fast AI picture he worries more about house prices than his job. The robot picture is the first where he can see himself being let go, and he pins his hopes on the shop counter.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because it's the first one that reaches him directly. He can picture his boss telling him on a Monday that a machine is cheaper.
whatWouldHelp: A robot tax that pays farm workers to retrain, and help for small farms to keep people on rather than grants that only go to machines.
